The Petty Conjecture for Convex Bodies of Revolution

Florian Mielke-Sulz ††thanks: Email: florian.mielkesulz@gmail.com
Abstract

The Petty conjecture asserts that the quotient Vn​(Π​K)/Vn​(K)n−1V_{n}(\Pi K)/V_{n}(K)^{n-1} is minimized among all convex bodies precisely by ellipsoids. In this paper, we prove the conjecture for all convex bodies of revolution in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥3n\geq 3, including the equality cases.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 52A40. Secondary 52A20, 52A38.
Keywords: Petty conjecture, projection body, body of revolution, affine isoperimetric inequality.

1  Introduction

Here and throughout, a convex body in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. For m≥1m\geq 1, we denote by VmV_{m} the mm-dimensional Lebesgue measure, by BmB^{m} the Euclidean unit ball in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, by κm=Vm​(Bm)\kappa_{m}=V_{m}(B^{m}) its volume, and by 𝕊m−1=∂Bm\mathbb{S}^{m-1}=\partial B^{m} the Euclidean unit sphere. Moreover, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the Euclidean inner product. The support function of a convex body KK is defined by

hK​(u)=maxx∈K⁡⟨x,u⟩,u∈𝕊n−1,h_{K}(u)=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle,\qquad u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1},

and its projection body Π​K\Pi K is the origin-symmetric convex body whose support function is given by

hΠ​K​(u)=Vn−1​(proju⟂⁡K),u∈𝕊n−1,h_{\Pi K}(u)=V_{n-1}\bigl(\operatorname{proj}_{u^{\perp}}K\bigr),\qquad u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1},

where proju⟂⁡K\operatorname{proj}_{u^{\perp}}K denotes the orthogonal projection of KK onto the hyperplane u⟂u^{\perp}.

The conjecture formulated by Petty [15] has been an open problem in convex geometry for decades [7]. For further background, see also [11].

Conjecture (Petty conjecture).

Let n≥3n\geq 3, let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body, and let Bn⊆ℝnB^{n}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be the Euclidean unit ball. Then

Vn​(Π​K)Vn​(K)n−1≥Vn​(Π​Bn)Vn​(Bn)n−1.\frac{V_{n}(\Pi K)}{V_{n}(K)^{n-1}}\geq\frac{V_{n}(\Pi B^{n})}{V_{n}(B^{n})^{n-1}}. (1)

Equality holds if and only if KK is an ellipsoid.

In a recent preprint, Chen, Feng, Li, Xi, and Xu prove the Petty conjecture in dimension three, including the equality cases [2]. For general convex bodies in dimensions n≥4n\geq 4, the conjecture remains open. Earlier partial results include results for certain classes of three-dimensional bodies [18], a local result for convex bodies with absolutely continuous surface area measure whose curvature function, after a linear transformation, is sufficiently close to the constant function 11 in L∞L^{\infty} [17], and a result under additional assumptions on the minimal surface area within the volume-preserving affine class [8]. Saroglou also showed that a classical proof approach based on Steiner symmetrization cannot work, since the Petty quotient Vn​(Π​K)/Vn​(K)n−1V_{n}(\Pi K)/V_{n}(K)^{n-1} is not monotone under Steiner symmetrization in general [18].

The class reduction due to Schneider [21] and extended by Lutwak [12] to projection bodies of different degrees shows that, after a suitable translation, every minimizer of the Petty quotient satisfies

Π2​K=α​Kfor some ​α>0,\Pi^{2}K=\alpha K\qquad\text{for some }\alpha>0,

where Π2​K=Π⁡(Π​K)\Pi^{2}K=\Pi(\Pi K). However, Weil showed that solutions of this equation need not be ellipsoids [23]. On the other hand, Ivaki proved that among the solutions of this equation for which hA​Kh_{AK} is sufficiently close to 11 in C2​(𝕊n−1)C^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}) for some invertible linear map AA, only origin-centered ellipsoids occur [10]. This local uniqueness result was subsequently generalized by Ortega-Moreno and Schuster to a broad class of sufficiently regular Minkowski valuations, further developing the fixed-point approach to the Petty conjecture [14].

A convex body K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a body of revolution if it is invariant under all rotations fixing some affine line pointwise. Since translations and orthogonal transformations preserve both the Petty quotient and the class of bodies of revolution, we may assume that this axis is ℝ​en\mathbb{R}e_{n}, where en=(0,…,0,1)e_{n}=(0,\ldots,0,1) denotes the nn-th standard basis vector. For bodies of revolution, Saroglou proved a non-sharp lower bound [19]. In dimensions n≥4n\geq 4, the sharp inequality together with its equality cases had remained open for this class. We prove the Petty conjecture, including its equality cases, for convex bodies of revolution in every dimension n≥3n\geq 3:

Main Result (Petty conjecture for convex bodies of revolution).

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body of revolution. Then (1) holds, with equality if and only if KK is an ellipsoid.

Independently, Dorrek found a proof of the same result with the assistance of AI and describes on his website how he arrived at it [4].

The proof presented in this paper begins with normalized Blaschke symmetrization, which preserves the projection body. By the Kneser–Süss inequality, this operation does not decrease volume and hence does not increase the Petty quotient. It therefore suffices to consider origin-symmetric bodies. After a suitable linear normalization, a smooth body of revolution K=−KK=-K has the representation

K={(x,z):x∈Bn−1,|z|≤f(|x|)},K=\{(x,z):x\in B^{n-1},\ |z|\leq f(|x|)\},

where ff is a concave boundary profile. The corresponding profile of the unit ball is f0​(r)=1−r2f_{0}(r)=\sqrt{1-r^{2}}. With y=rn−1y=r^{n-1}, set

bK​(y)=−f′​(y1/(n−1)),b0​(y)=−f0′​(y1/(n−1)).b_{K}(y)=-f^{\prime}(y^{1/(n-1)}),\qquad b_{0}(y)=-f_{0}^{\prime}(y^{1/(n-1)}).

Writing g=bK/b0g=b_{K}/b_{0} and bg=g​b0=bKb_{g}=gb_{0}=b_{K}, we introduce integral functionals II and TT satisfying

Vn​(K)=2​κn−1n−1​I​(bg),Vn​(Π​K)=2n​κn−1nn!​T​(bg),V_{n}(K)=\frac{2\kappa_{n-1}}{n-1}I(b_{g}),\qquad V_{n}(\Pi K)=\frac{2^{n}\kappa_{n-1}^{\,n}}{n!}T(b_{g}),

where the first identity follows from integration by parts and the second from the volume formula for zonoids. Comparison with the unit ball reduces (1) to the analytic inequality

T⁡(bg)T⁡(b0)≥(I⁡(bg)I⁡(b0))n−1.\frac{T(b_{g})}{T(b_{0})}\geq\left(\frac{I(b_{g})}{I(b_{0})}\right)^{n-1}.

A determinant estimate reduces this inequality to a lower bound for a multilinear functional ℬ\mathcal{B}. The spherical Blaschke–Petkantschin formula expresses its diagonal in terms of determinants of moment matrices. Rotational symmetry reduces these determinants to the axial and transverse eigenvalues. Integration by parts then yields a weighted integral of αgn−1\alpha_{g}^{n-1}, where αg\alpha_{g} is a scalar integral transform of gg. Hölder’s inequality gives the required bound.

This proves the inequality for smooth bodies and, by approximation, for arbitrary bodies of revolution. For the nonsmooth equality case, we introduce profile measures ρK\rho_{K} and ρ0\rho_{0}, which also capture cylindrical boundary parts. The equality condition in Hölder’s inequality and the injectivity of the extended transform imply ρK=c​ρ0\rho_{K}=c\rho_{0}, which characterizes the ellipsoidal profile. Finally, equality in the Kneser–Süss inequality shows that the original body is a translate of its Blaschke symmetral, which completes the characterization of equality.

2  Notation and Preliminaries

d​σ¯m=d​σm(m+1)​κm+1\,\mathrm{d}\overline{\sigma}_{m}=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{m}}{(m+1)\kappa_{m+1}}

be the associated rotation-invariant probability measure. By projE\operatorname{proj}_{E} we denote the orthogonal projection onto a linear subspace EE, by u⟂u^{\perp} the orthogonal complement of u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, by ℋm\mathcal{H}^{m} the mm-dimensional Hausdorff measure, by G⁡(n,k)G(n,k) the Grassmannian of kk-dimensional linear subspaces of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and by GL⁡(n)\operatorname{GL}(n) the group of invertible linear transformations on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For A∈GL⁡(n)A\in\operatorname{GL}(n), we set A−T=(A−1)TA^{-T}=(A^{-1})^{T}.

A zonotope is a finite Minkowski sum of line segments. A convex body is called a zonoid if it is a limit of zonotopes in the Hausdorff metric. Every projection body is an origin-symmetric zonoid.

We denote the surface area measure of a convex body KK by SKS_{K}. By the existence and uniqueness theorem for the Minkowski problem, the Blaschke sum K​#​LK\#L is determined up to translation by SK​#​L=SK+SLS_{K\#L}=S_{K}+S_{L}. We denote by KBK^{\mathrm{B}} the origin-symmetric representative of the normalized Blaschke sum 2−1/(n−1)(K#(−K))2^{-1/(n-1)}(K\#(-K)), that is,

KB=2−1/(n−1)(K#(−K)).K^{\mathrm{B}}=2^{-1/(n-1)}(K\#(-K)). (2)

Finally, C+∞C^{\infty}_{+} denotes the class of convex bodies KK whose boundary ∂K\partial K is a C∞C^{\infty} hypersurface with everywhere positive Gaussian curvature. Bodies in this class will be called smooth. For further background on these notions, we refer the reader to Schneider [22].

3  The Analytic Inequality

The analytic core of the proof is the comparison of the functionals TT and II established in Lemma 3.5. It is based on the determinant estimate in Lemma 3.1, the factorization of ℬ\mathcal{B} in Lemma 3.3, and Hölder’s inequality.

Lemma 3.1 (Determinant estimate).

Let g∈C⁡([0,1])g\in C([0,1]) be nonnegative. Then

T⁡(bg)≥n​ℬ​(g,…,g).T(b_{g})\geq n\,\mathcal{B}(g,\ldots,g).

If gg is constant, then equality holds. In particular,

T⁡(b0)=n​ℬ​(1,…,1).T(b_{0})=n\,\mathcal{B}(1,\ldots,1).

The classical Blaschke–Petkantschin formulas decompose integrals over tuples of points according to the linear or affine subspaces they span [20, Section 7.2]. To factorize ℬ\mathcal{B}, we use the following spherical version [1, Lemma 3.2]. The extension from nonnegative to integrable functions follows by considering the positive and negative parts separately.

Lemma 3.2 (Spherical Blaschke–Petkantschin formula).

Let F:(𝕊n−1)n−1→ℝF\colon(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})^{n-1}\to\mathbb{R} be integrable. Then

∫(𝕊n−1)n−1F(u1,…,un−1)dσn−1(u1)⋯dσn−1(un−1)\displaystyle\int_{(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})^{n-1}}F(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n-1})\,\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{n-1}(u_{1})\cdots\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{n-1}(u_{n-1})
=n​κn2​∫G⁡(n,n−1)∫(𝕊n−1∩H)n−1F⁡(u1,…,un−1)​Δ​(u1,…,un−1)\displaystyle=\frac{n\kappa_{n}}{2}\int_{G(n,n-1)}\int_{(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\cap H)^{n-1}}F(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n-1})\Delta(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n-1})
dσH(u1)⋯dσH(un−1)dH,\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\sigma_{H}(u_{1})\cdots\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{H}(u_{n-1})\,\,\mathrm{d}H,

where d​σH\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{H} denotes surface measure on 𝕊n−1∩H\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\cap H, and d​H\,\mathrm{d}H denotes the rotation-invariant probability measure on G⁡(n,n−1)G(n,n-1).

To state and prove the factorization lemma below, we introduce the following notation. For g∈C⁡([0,1])g\in C([0,1]) and 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1, set

αg​(t)=κn−2​∫−11g⁡((1−t2​s2)(n−1)/2)​(1−s2)(n−2)/2​𝑑s.\alpha_{g}(t)=\kappa_{n-2}\int_{-1}^{1}g\bigl((1-t^{2}s^{2})^{(n-1)/2}\bigr)(1-s^{2})^{(n-2)/2}\,\,\mathrm{d}s. (11)
Lemma 3.3 (Factorization of ℬ\mathcal{B}).

There exists a constant cn>0c_{n}>0 depending only on the dimension such that, for all g1,…,gn−1∈C⁡([0,1])g_{1},\ldots,g_{n-1}\in C([0,1]),

ℬ(g1,…,gn−1)=cn∫01tn1−t2αg1(t)⋯αgn−1(t)dt.\mathcal{B}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{n-1})=c_{n}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{n}}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}\,\alpha_{g_{1}}(t)\cdots\alpha_{g_{n-1}}(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t. (12)

Moreover,

Lemma 3.4 (Injectivity of g↦αgg\mapsto\alpha_{g}).

The linear operator

C⁡([0,1])→C⁡([0,1]),g↦αg,C([0,1])\to C([0,1]),\qquad g\mapsto\alpha_{g},

is injective.

Proof.

Let g∈C⁡([0,1])g\in C([0,1]) with αg≡0\alpha_{g}\equiv 0. The substitutions z=t2z=t^{2} and u=z​s2u=zs^{2} in the one-dimensional representation (11) of αg\alpha_{g} yield, for 0<z≤10<z\leq 1,

z(n−1)/2αg(z)=Cn∫0z(z−u)(n−2)/2u−1/2g((1−u)(n−1)/2)duz^{(n-1)/2}\alpha_{g}(\sqrt{z})=C_{n}\int_{0}^{z}(z-u)^{(n-2)/2}u^{-1/2}g\bigl((1-u)^{(n-1)/2}\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}u (16)

with a constant Cn>0C_{n}>0.

For 0<u≤10<u\leq 1, set

h(u)=u−1/2g((1−u)(n−1)/2),h(u)=u^{-1/2}g\bigl((1-u)^{(n-1)/2}\bigr),

and set h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0. Since gg is bounded, we have h∈L1​([0,1])h\in L^{1}([0,1]). Let Γ\Gamma denote the gamma function and let ℐβ\mathcal{I}^{\beta} be the normalized Riemann–Liouville fractional integral

(ℐβ​h)​(z)=1Γ⁡(β)​∫0z(z−u)β−1​h​(u)​𝑑u,β>0.(\mathcal{I}^{\beta}h)(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_{0}^{z}(z-u)^{\beta-1}h(u)\,\,\mathrm{d}u,\qquad\beta>0.

ℐn/2​h=0.\mathcal{I}^{n/2}h=0.

Choose an integer k>n/2k>n/2. By the semigroup property of the Riemann–Liouville fractional integrals [16, Theorem 2.5],

ℐk​h=ℐk−n/2​ℐn/2​h=0\mathcal{I}^{k}h=\mathcal{I}^{k-n/2}\mathcal{I}^{n/2}h=0

almost everywhere on (0,1)(0,1). For integer kk, the formula for repeated integration gives

dkd​zk​ℐk​h=h\frac{\,\mathrm{d}^{k}}{\,\mathrm{d}z^{k}}\mathcal{I}^{k}h=h

in the sense of distributions on (0,1)(0,1). Hence, h=0h=0 almost everywhere.

Since

g⁡((1−u)(n−1)/2)=u1/2​h​(u),0<u≤1,g\bigl((1-u)^{(n-1)/2}\bigr)=u^{1/2}h(u),\qquad 0<u\leq 1,

With these preparations, we can now prove the analytic inequality, characterize its equality cases, and then use it to derive the Petty inequality for convex bodies of revolution.

Lemma 3.5 (Analytic inequality).

For every continuous function g:[0,1]→[0,∞)g\colon[0,1]\to[0,\infty),

T⁡(bg)T⁡(b0)≥(I⁡(bg)I⁡(b0))n−1.\frac{T(b_{g})}{T(b_{0})}\geq\left(\frac{I(b_{g})}{I(b_{0})}\right)^{n-1}. (17)

Equality holds if and only if gg is constant.

Proof.

Since g≥0g\geq 0, we have αg≥0\alpha_{g}\geq 0. Applying Hölder’s inequality to the integral representation in Lemma 3.3, with weight

tn1−t2\frac{t^{n}}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}

and exponents n−1n-1 and (n−1)/(n−2)(n-1)/(n-2), yields

ℬ​(g,1,…,1)n−1≤ℬ⁡(g,…,g)​ℬ​(1,…,1)n−2.\mathcal{B}(g,1,\ldots,1)^{n-1}\leq\mathcal{B}(g,\ldots,g)\mathcal{B}(1,\ldots,1)^{n-2}. (18)

Since ℬ⁡(1,…,1)>0\mathcal{B}(1,\ldots,1)>0, Lemma 3.1 and (13) yield

T⁡(bg)T⁡(b0)\displaystyle\frac{T(b_{g})}{T(b_{0})} ≥ℬ⁡(g,…,g)ℬ⁡(1,…,1)\displaystyle\geq\frac{\mathcal{B}(g,\ldots,g)}{\mathcal{B}(1,\ldots,1)}
≥(ℬ⁡(g,1,…,1)ℬ⁡(1,…,1))n−1\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{\mathcal{B}(g,1,\ldots,1)}{\mathcal{B}(1,\ldots,1)}\right)^{n-1}
=(I⁡(bg)I⁡(b0))n−1.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{I(b_{g})}{I(b_{0})}\right)^{n-1}.

If equality holds, then equality must in particular hold in (18). Since the weight in the Hölder inequality is positive almost everywhere and α1\alpha_{1} is a positive constant, the equality case in Hölder’s inequality, see [9, Problem 7.2.15], gives

αg​(t)=c​α1​(t)\alpha_{g}(t)=c\,\alpha_{1}(t)

for almost every t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) and some c≥0c\geq 0. By continuity, this identity holds on all of [0,1][0,1]. Linearity and Lemma 3.4 therefore yield αg−c=0\alpha_{g-c}=0, and hence g≡cg\equiv c.

Conversely, if g≡cg\equiv c with c≥0c\geq 0, then bg=c​b0b_{g}=cb_{0}. By the homogeneity of TT and II,

T⁡(bg)=cn−1​T​(b0),I⁡(bg)=c​I​(b0),T(b_{g})=c^{n-1}T(b_{0}),\qquad I(b_{g})=cI(b_{0}),

and hence equality holds in the stated inequality. ∎

4  Smooth Convex Bodies of Revolution

We first replace KK by the normalized Blaschke sum 2−1/(n−1)(K#(−K))2^{-1/(n-1)}(K\#(-K)), which is origin-symmetric, has the same projection body as KK, and does not decrease its volume. After this reduction and a suitable linear normalization, we use the functionals II and TT to translate the analytic inequality (17) into the corresponding geometric inequality for Vn​(K)V_{n}(K) and Vn​(Π​K)V_{n}(\Pi K).

To express Vn​(Π​K)V_{n}(\Pi K) in terms of TT, we use the following volume formula for zonoids.

Lemma 4.1 (Volume formula for zonoids).

Let (X,μ)(X,\mu) be a finite measure space and let q:X→ℝnq\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^{n} be integrable. If the zonoid Z⊆ℝnZ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is defined by

hZ​(u)=∫X|⟨u,q⁡(x)⟩|​𝑑μ​(x),u∈𝕊n−1,h_{Z}(u)=\int_{X}|\langle u,q(x)\rangle|\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x),\qquad u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1},

then

Vn(Z)=2nn!∫Xn|det(q(x1),…,q(xn))|dμ(x1)⋯dμ(xn).V_{n}(Z)=\frac{2^{n}}{n!}\int_{X^{n}}\left|\det\bigl(q(x_{1}),\ldots,q(x_{n})\bigr)\right|\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x_{1})\cdots\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x_{n}).
Proof.

Set q^​(x)=q⁡(x)/‖q⁡(x)‖\widehat{q}(x)=q(x)/\|q(x)\| whenever q⁡(x)≠0q(x)\neq 0, and q^​(x)=en\widehat{q}(x)=e_{n} otherwise. Define a finite even Borel measure ν\nu on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} by

∫𝕊n−1f⁡(v)​𝑑ν​(v)=12​∫X‖q⁡(x)‖​(f⁡(q^​(x))+f⁡(−q^​(x)))​𝑑μ​(x)\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}f(v)\,\,\mathrm{d}\nu(v)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{X}\|q(x)\|\bigl(f(\widehat{q}(x))+f(-\widehat{q}(x))\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)

for f∈C⁡(𝕊n−1)f\in C(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}). Then

hZ​(u)=∫𝕊n−1|⟨u,v⟩|​𝑑ν​(v),h_{Z}(u)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}|\langle u,v\rangle|\,\,\mathrm{d}\nu(v),

so ν\nu is a generating measure of ZZ. The volume formula for zonoids [22, Theorem 5.3.2, in particular (5.82)] therefore gives

Vn(Z)=2nn!∫(𝕊n−1)n|det(v1,…,vn)|dν(v1)⋯dν(vn).V_{n}(Z)=\frac{2^{n}}{n!}\int_{(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})^{n}}|\det(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})|\,\,\mathrm{d}\nu(v_{1})\cdots\,\mathrm{d}\nu(v_{n}).

By the definition of ν\nu and the invariance of the absolute determinant under sign changes, the last integral equals

∫Xn|det(q(x1),…,q(xn))|dμ(x1)⋯dμ(xn),\int_{X^{n}}\left|\det\bigl(q(x_{1}),\ldots,q(x_{n})\bigr)\right|\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x_{1})\cdots\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x_{n}),

which proves the claim. ∎

Theorem 4.2 (Smooth case for convex bodies of revolution).

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body of revolution of class C+∞C^{\infty}_{+}. Then

Vn​(Π​K)≥κn−1nκnn−2​Vn​(K)n−1.V_{n}(\Pi K)\geq\frac{\kappa_{n-1}^{\,n}}{\kappa_{n}^{\,n-2}}V_{n}(K)^{n-1}. (19)

Equality holds if and only if KK is an ellipsoid.

Proof.

5  Profile Measures and the Nonsmooth Equality Case

6  Proof of the Main Result

We now combine the results of the preceding sections. The inequality follows by smooth approximation, while the characterization of the equality case is based on the profile measure statement proved above.

Theorem 6.1 (Petty conjecture for convex bodies of revolution).

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body of revolution. Then

Vn​(Π​K)≥κn−1nκnn−2​Vn​(K)n−1.V_{n}(\Pi K)\geq\frac{\kappa_{n-1}^{\,n}}{\kappa_{n}^{\,n-2}}V_{n}(K)^{n-1}. (31)

Equality holds if and only if KK is an ellipsoid.

Proof.

By smoothing the support function while preserving rotational symmetry and adding a vanishing Euclidean ball, we choose convex bodies of revolution KjK_{j} of class C+∞C^{\infty}_{+} with Kj→KK_{j}\to K in the Hausdorff metric. By Theorem 4.2,

Vn​(Π​Kj)≥κn−1nκnn−2​Vn​(Kj)n−1.V_{n}(\Pi K_{j})\geq\frac{\kappa_{n-1}^{\,n}}{\kappa_{n}^{\,n-2}}V_{n}(K_{j})^{n-1}.

The continuity of volume and of the projection body operator yields the stated inequality for KK upon passing to the limit.

We now consider the equality case. Let KBK^{\mathrm{B}} be the Blaschke symmetral from (2), which is again a body of revolution. As in the first step of the proof of Theorem 4.2, we have Π​KB=Π​K\Pi K^{\mathrm{B}}=\Pi K and Vn​(KB)≥Vn​(K)V_{n}(K^{\mathrm{B}})\geq V_{n}(K). Both statements hold without any regularity assumption. Comparing the Petty inequality for KBK^{\mathrm{B}} with equality for KK gives Vn​(KB)=Vn​(K)V_{n}(K^{\mathrm{B}})=V_{n}(K) and equality for KBK^{\mathrm{B}}.

After a scaling in en⟂e_{n}^{\perp}, we may assume that projen⟂⁡KB=Bn−1.\operatorname{proj}_{e_{n}^{\perp}}K^{\mathrm{B}}=B^{n-1}. Let f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\to[0,\infty) denote the boundary profile of the normalized body KBK^{\mathrm{B}} from Definition 5.1. The two outer terms in the chain (25) from Proposition 5.3 then agree, so equality also holds in the second inequality. Consequently, ρKB=c​ρ0\rho_{K^{\mathrm{B}}}=c\rho_{0} for some c>0c>0. Since ρ0\rho_{0} has no atom at 11, we first obtain f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0. If we compare the absolutely continuous parts of the identity ρKB=c​ρ0\rho_{K^{\mathrm{B}}}=c\rho_{0}, we obtain

bKB​(y)​y1/(n−1)=c​y2/(n−1)1−y2/(n−1)b_{K^{\mathrm{B}}}(y)y^{1/(n-1)}=c\frac{y^{2/(n-1)}}{\sqrt{1-y^{2/(n-1)}}}

for almost every y∈(0,1)y\in(0,1). Thus, with the substitution r=y1/(n−1)r=y^{1/(n-1)}, we obtain

−f′​(r)=c​r1−r2-f^{\prime}(r)=c\frac{r}{\sqrt{1-r^{2}}}

for almost every r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1). Hence, f⁡(r)=c​1−r2f(r)=c\sqrt{1-r^{2}}, and the normalized image of KBK^{\mathrm{B}} is an ellipsoid of revolution. Consequently, the original body KBK^{\mathrm{B}} is an ellipsoid.

The equality Vn​(KB)=Vn​(K)V_{n}(K^{\mathrm{B}})=V_{n}(K), established before normalization, gives equality in (20). The argument at the end of the proof of Theorem 4.2 applies without any regularity assumption and shows that KK is a translate of KBK^{\mathrm{B}}. Thus, KK is an ellipsoid.

Conversely, every ellipsoid attains equality in (31), by affine invariance of the Petty quotient. ∎

Corollary 6.2 (Affine extension).

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body whose Blaschke symmetral KBK^{\mathrm{B}} is affinely equivalent to a body of revolution. Then (31) holds, with equality if and only if KK is an ellipsoid.

The assumption on KBK^{\mathrm{B}} is equivalent to requiring Π​K\Pi K to be linearly equivalent to a body of revolution.

Proof.

For A∈GL⁡(n)A\in\operatorname{GL}(n), the transformation formula

Π⁡(A​K)=|detA|​A−T​Π​K\Pi(AK)=|\det A|A^{-T}\Pi K

and translation invariance imply that the Petty quotient is affine invariant. Thus, Theorem 6.1 applies to a suitable affine image of KBK^{\mathrm{B}}. Together with Π​KB=Π​K\Pi K^{\mathrm{B}}=\Pi K and (20), this gives

Vn​(Π​K)Vn​(K)n−1≥Vn​(Π​KB)Vn​(KB)n−1≥κn−1nκnn−2.\frac{V_{n}(\Pi K)}{V_{n}(K)^{n-1}}\geq\frac{V_{n}(\Pi K^{\mathrm{B}})}{V_{n}(K^{\mathrm{B}})^{n-1}}\geq\frac{\kappa_{n-1}^{\,n}}{\kappa_{n}^{\,n-2}}.

Equality forces KBK^{\mathrm{B}} to be an ellipsoid and equality in (20). The argument at the end of the proof of Theorem 4.2 then shows that KK is a translate of KBK^{\mathrm{B}}, hence an ellipsoid. Conversely, ellipsoids attain equality by affine invariance.

It remains to prove the equivalence of the two assumptions. One implication follows from the transformation formula, the identity Π​KB=Π​K\Pi K^{\mathrm{B}}=\Pi K, and the fact that the projection body of a body of revolution is again a body of revolution. Conversely, suppose that T​Π​KT\Pi K is a body of revolution for some T∈GL⁡(n)T\in\operatorname{GL}(n), and set A=|detT|1/(n−1)​T−TA=|\det T|^{1/(n-1)}T^{-T}. Then Π⁡(A​KB)=T​Π​K\Pi(AK^{\mathrm{B}})=T\Pi K. Since this body is origin-symmetric, its axis passes through the origin. For every rotation RR fixing this axis pointwise,

Π⁡(R​A​KB)=R​Π​(A​KB)=Π⁡(A​KB).\Pi(RAK^{\mathrm{B}})=R\Pi(AK^{\mathrm{B}})=\Pi(AK^{\mathrm{B}}).

The injectivity of the projection body operator on origin-symmetric convex bodies [6, Theorem 3.3.6] yields R​A​KB=A​KBRAK^{\mathrm{B}}=AK^{\mathrm{B}}. Hence, A​KBAK^{\mathrm{B}} is a body of revolution. ∎
